title: How do you implement a custom watermark strategy (implement WatermarkStrategy with createTimestampAssigner and createWatermarkGenerator), and what is the impact of setting max-out-of-orderness too high (high latency) vs too low (dropped events)?
shortTitle: How do you implement a custom watermark strategy

s1_definition.oneliner: A custom watermark strategy pairs a timestamp extractor with a watermark generator that decides when and how far to advance the watermark, and the out-of-orderness setting is the dial between waiting too long and dropping too much.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **WatermarkStrategy interface** – A factory that supplies two collaborators: a `TimestampAssigner` to extract event time from each record and a `WatermarkGenerator` to advance the watermark.
- **TimestampAssigner** – Pulls the event-time millis from each record, e.g. `(event, ts) -> event.getEventTimeMillis()`.
- **Periodic generator** – Emits watermarks on a fixed interval via `onPeriodicEmit`, using max-seen minus a delay; the built-in `forBoundedOutOfOrderness` is a periodic generator.
- **Punctuated generator** – Emits watermarks in response to specific marker events inside `onEvent`, useful when the source has explicit batch-completion markers.
- **Out-of-orderness trade-off** – Too high adds latency and holds more state; too low drops legitimate late events, understating results.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India needs a rule for when to declare a business minute closed. The timestamp assigner is the clerk who reads the true time off each transaction slip. The watermark generator is the policy that says "announce the minute closed once we are confident all slips for it have arrived." If the policy waits a very long time, the report is late. If it closes too eagerly, slips that were just a few seconds behind get thrown away. A custom strategy lets the bank write its own closing rule.

```text
  Custom Watermark Strategy Components

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WatermarkStrategy<Transaction>           │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │                                          │
  │  createTimestampAssigner()               │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ TimestampAssigner                │    │
  │  │ (txn, ts) -> txn.getEventTime() │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                          │
  │  createWatermarkGenerator()              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ WatermarkGenerator               │    │
  │  │ onEvent: track maxTimestamp      │    │
  │  │ onPeriodicEmit: emit WM          │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Out-of-orderness spectrum:
  ◀── EAGER (low delay)         RELAXED (high delay) ──▶
  Fast results                  Complete results
  Drops late events             Catches late events
  Low memory                    High memory
  Use for: alerts               Use for: settlements
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A custom watermark strategy in Flink is how you take control of event-time progress when the built-in strategies are not enough. You implement the `WatermarkStrategy` interface, which is a factory for two collaborators: a timestamp assigner that pulls the event-time timestamp from each record, and a watermark generator that decides when to advance the watermark.

A periodic generator emits the watermark on a fixed interval, which is how the built-in bounded-out-of-orderness strategy works. A punctuated generator emits a watermark directly inside `onEvent` when it sees a special marker record, which is ideal when your source has explicit completeness markers like an end-of-batch record, because you can advance time exactly when the data guarantees a batch is finished.

The out-of-orderness setting is the dial everyone must understand. Too high means every window waits longer, increasing latency and memory. Too low means slightly-delayed events are dropped, silently understating results. The professional approach is to measure the real lateness distribution, set the out-of-orderness to the 99th percentile, and handle the rare tail with allowed lateness and a side output.

At the National Bank of India the nightly settlement feed arrived in explicit batches, each ending with an end-of-batch marker, so Rajesh wrote a punctuated custom strategy that advanced the watermark the instant the marker arrived, removing the latency of a fixed time delay while guaranteeing completeness. He also protected against idle partitions with `withIdleness` so a stalled source did not freeze all windows.

Remember one sentence: The watermark strategy pairs a timestamp extractor with a generator that advances the watermark, and the out-of-orderness dial trades latency against completeness, so measure your data's real delay rather than guessing.

---

keyPoints: WatermarkStrategy is a factory for a TimestampAssigner (extracts event time) and a WatermarkGenerator (advances the watermark).
A periodic generator emits watermarks on a fixed interval; the built-in forBoundedOutOfOrderness is a periodic generator.
A punctuated generator emits watermarks in response to specific marker events, ideal for sources with explicit batch-completion markers.
Out-of-orderness too high increases latency and memory; too low drops legitimate late events and understates results.
Measure the real lateness distribution and set out-of-orderness to the 99th percentile, handling the tail with allowed lateness and side outputs.
Use withIdleness to prevent an idle partition from holding back the global watermark and freezing all windows.
